messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Authority Presence: Police, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Drug Use: take drugs, Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Priya was pulling her sedan into the loading lane behind the convenience store on Elm Street when a man stepped out from between two delivery trucks. He did not ask. He pressed something cold against her ribs, told her to keep her hands visible, and ordered her to unlock the glove compartment. She obeyed because her legs had locked, because the voice was low and immediate, because he shifted his weight and she knew hesitation would cost her more. He took her wallet, her phone, and her delivery tablet. He told her to drive away slowly, that he was watching. She did. In the weeks that followed, Priya’s mind offered the encounter in fragments. She kept seeing the scuff of the man’s boots against the asphalt, the glare of the streetlamp catching metal, the way his jacket zipped halfway up his chest. When she closed her eyes, she heard the sharp crack of his lighter, the metallic click of the lock snapping back, the low rumble of his warning. Some nights, none of that came at all. She would simply jolt awake, her chest tight, her pulse hammering with the exact same terror, though she could not recall a single picture or sound. The memory stayed fixed on the key turning in the ignition, on her own silence. She would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened. The guilt sat heavy in her stomach. She stopped answering messages from her cousins in Flushing, stopped going to the community center. She felt cut off, as if a glass wall now separated her from everyone else. At the same time, she told herself over and over that it was fine, that it wasn’t really that bad, that she was lucky she walked away. The words felt hollow, but she kept repeating them until the memory blurred. Comfort became impossible. Before walking into any building, Priya’s eyes scanned for exits, counting doors, noting which stairwells were locked. She parked her car facing the street, never back in, so she could bolt forward if she needed to. When a delivery courier stood too still near the loading dock, Priya’s stomach dropped. She couldn’t look at him. She turned her cart around and walked away. At night, she woke at least twice, sitting up in bed to listen for footsteps, to check that the deadbolt was still thrown. Even in her own apartment, with the windows shut and the radiator hissing, her shoulders stayed braced. She could not let go. Her work environment held its own weight. As a delivery driver, she spent her days navigating gridlocked streets and tight alleyways. One Tuesday, a police cruiser pulled up alongside her at an intersection. The officer leaned out, asking for her registration. Priya’s breath stopped. Her hands gripped the steering wheel until her knuckles went white. She could not speak. She just nodded, hands trembling, and drove off the moment the light turned green. After that, she stopped driving. She asked her supervisor to switch her to warehouse sorting. When she tried to ride in a coworker’s car to visit her sister, her throat closed, her vision tunneled, and she begged to be let out at the first stop. She started taking pills before work, just enough to quiet the noise in her head, just enough to sleep. At twenty-two, Priya walked into the clinic with her coat pulled tight and her eyes fixed on the floor. She had come because the warehouse shelves made her nauseous, because she kept waking up gasping, because the pills were not working anymore. She said she just wanted to know how to stop feeling like the world was always one wrong turn away from collapsing. She hoped, quietly, to be able to drive again. She was most afraid, though, that no matter what she did, she would never be able to stop the bad things from finding her.
